_about:
DECISIONS HE MADE IN CHAT — the one hole the five swept sources cannot reach. A decision said in conversation and never written into a changelog, a standard or a workbook is in no file, so no sweep can find it. It is recorded HERE the same day, in his words, and the extractor folds it into the decision log beside the rest. This file is hand-written on purpose: it is the only place in the log that is.

AND WHICH NUMBERED QUESTION EACH ONE ANSWERS (2026-09-30). Founder: “when I asked you to create one decision log and other files recording all decision no matter where I make that decision - how does not include updating with questions I am answering - they are not decision in your mind or what?” His answers to Q51, Q52 and Q53 WERE in the decision log from the moment he gave them — what I never did was carry them into the other file that holds the same decision, the master's own answer column, which is his PFS rule. Then I fixed it by inventing a SECOND home for answers, which is how two files come to disagree. So an answer names its question HERE, in the one log, and the master's answer column is printed from this file. One decision, one place, every destination fed from it.

rows.plain:
Noted 2026-10-22, what the screen shows now: his DEC-1669 (2026-10-04, every return time-weighted) replaced this — the money-weighted rate described below no longer stands in, and the window Return it was compared with was removed the same day. Where the Return cannot be measured, the Performance tab and the account page show no percent and a sentence saying why, never another method (MK-PF-M-016, MK-PF-M-017). — TODAY, when money moved in or out in amounts large enough that WHEN it moved would decide the percentage, the Return states nothing and the screen shows the dollar walk alone. That person — someone actively adding money — is the one who most needs a rate and currently never sees one.
HIS RULING: show the exact rate there instead. Where the walk now says there is no percentage, it will read that counting when you added money, the rate was X% a year.
WHY THIS IS SAFE, measured: the two methods are not different answers. The window Return divides the gain once by a straight-line average of the money at work; the money-weighted rate compounds each amount over its own days and solves for the rate. On $100,000 with $10,000 added on 1 July and $118,000 at the end, they give 7.6161% and 7.6341% — 0.018 of a percentage point apart. They can never be far apart, because the window Return REFUSES the moment its straight-line shortcut could be off by more than a percentage point. So this fills the gap it leaves and never contradicts it: one return is visible at a time.
WHERE IT CAME FROM: the figure was built 2026-07-14 as its own card on the old Invest screen, and the Performance design he approved on 2026-09-25 (mock v14) removed that card. The function has been correct and reached by no screen since.

rows.subject: In the time-weighted return, money that moves on a day counts for that whole day
rows.plain: The time-weighted return counts money that arrives on a day as there for that whole day, and money taken out as gone for that whole day: that day's growth is the evening value ÷ (the previous evening's value + money added − money taken out) − 1. A new account opened with $10,000 and worth $10,050 that evening returned +0.50% that day (+$50); worth $9,800, −2.00% (−$200). Vanguard worth $50,000, $10,000 added in the morning, $60,300 that evening: +0.50% (the $300 was earned on $60,000). Before: the money counted as arriving at the end of the day — the first deposit into a new account could not be measured at all, a value below the money just added was refused as a broken record, and the Vanguard day read +0.60%.
rows.means: Said in chat on 2026-10-11, approving my recommendation after he asked why a $10,000 first deposit worth $10,050 that evening showed no return. A refinement of how DEC-1669's time-weighted return splits at a movement; DEC-1669 stands.

rows.subject: Let price history count: a window that starts before the daily record is worked back from each holding's price history and what is left out is named, rather than greyed
rows.plain: Let price history count. When a period starts before the daily record, work it back from each holding's price history and name what's left out, rather than greying it. No balance is invented, because the figures come from real prices, so DEC-0230 still holds for the values you typed. The day-one line would change to say the figures come from price history. Example: Vanguard linked today, VTI $40,000 with a year of prices (+10%), Treasury 2031 $10,000 typed by hand; the daily record begins today. Tap 1Y: the button reads +10.00% (not greyed), Wealth generated $3,636 (40,000 × (1 − 1 ÷ 1.10)), Return +10.00% (VTI only), and below: "Wealth generated and Return do not include Treasury 2031's gains, as it has no price history." Before: greyed "—" and "The record begins Oct 13, 2026, so it cannot say what these accounts were worth on Oct 12, 2025."
rows.means: His recommendation, approved in chat on 2026-10-13 with the word "approved." It replaces DEC-3035i (2026-10-07: "Performance draws no walk for a window its record exists but cannot reach; a sentence names the record's first day"). A window whose beginning the daily record cannot read is now worked back by the DEC-3656 / DEC-5068 path whether or not a record exists: beginning = today's value − each holding's known gain − money put in + money taken out; Return = the return of the holdings with a history (knownHoldingsReturn); a holding with no history adds $0 and is named. DEC-3035i's sentence ("The record begins …, so it cannot say what this account was / these accounts were worth on …") still shows, and the window is still greyed, only where NO holding in that window has a history — nothing real to work back from, so a typed value is never carried back to a day nobody recorded (DEC-0230 holds). Cash (uninvested cash, a cash position) gains $0, is not named as "no price history", and is not in Return. A window the record DOES reach keeps the measured time-weighted return (DEC-4439), unchanged. SOME ACCOUNTS REACH, SOME DO NOT: the accounts the record reaches are read and measured together as before (an account with no history that joined the record late still arrives as money put in, DEC-4439); each account it does not reach that has a holding with a history is worked back on its own, exactly as its card is; the summary is these parts added up, so every walk line of the summary equals the same line on those cards added up (an account whose card is greyed adds only its value now). Return there = Σ values now ÷ Σ (value now ÷ (1 + return)) − 1 over the reached accounts together (their measured return) and each worked-back holding with a history. DAY-ONE LINE: where any longer window is worked back, "You added your accounts today. Figures for 1M, 1Y and longer come from each holding's past prices." (his words, approved 2026-10-14 as DEC-5425; the words first proposed here were replaced); on a true day one with no holding history v17's words stand.

rows.subject: A bond's or CD's return counts the interest it paid; its line shows face, coupon and YTM; the account page's window bar shows the app's own figures
rows.plain: Three parts. (a) A bond's or CD's return over a window is its price change PLUS the interest it was paid in the window: interest and coupon records dated on or after the window's first day that name that holding (or, naming no holding, sit in an account that is that one bond or CD). Return = (1 + price change) × (1 + interest ÷ value today) − 1, which is (value today + interest) ÷ value at the start − 1. KeyBank CD $5,000, price flat, $100 interest → +2.00%; US Treasury $4,000, $85 → +2.125%, shown +2.13%; the Bonds & CDs bar $9,000, $185 → +2.06%. Only an individual bond or CD counts its interest this way (Bonds & CDs, no fund word in its name, not a Treasury-bill ETF, and a CD type, a 9-character security id, a maturity date, a coupon rate or a face value to say it is one instrument); a bond fund's distributions are already in its adjusted closes (DEC-4644), so nothing is counted twice. An account's own time-weighted return (DEC-4439) measures its whole value, the interest that landed in its cash included, and does not change. (b) The columns keep one meaning each (DEC-0093): MARKET VALUE is market value and adds up to the account; RETURN is the window return with interest. The line under a bond's or CD's name shows its face value, coupon rate and yield to maturity, as a stock's shows its shares: $5,000 face · 4.00% · YTM 4.00%. A bank CD's yield to maturity is its rate; a part not given is left out. (c) The account-page drawing's window bar on every state (A to E) is the app's own figure, read off the built screen with each state's data; a window the app greys is a dash, and the grey placeholders are gone.
rows.means: His two points, 2026-10-19, and his word approved on the recommendation. rows.subject: A window that opens before the daily record begins is joined at the record's first day: the days before it are worked back from price history, then the record's own return
rows.plain: Where a window's first day is before the daily record begins, its return is two parts multiplied: the days before the record's first day, worked back from each holding's price history (holdings with a history only, DEC-5068 and DEC-5291; a bond's or CD's interest added, DEC-6212), and the record's own time-weighted return from its first day to today (DEC-4439), the one Since shows. Return = (1 + the days before) × (1 + the record's part) − 1. The walk is joined the same way: its beginning is the record's first value worked back over the days before it (less what the holdings gained then and the money moved then), then the record's walk; it still adds up to today's ending. Only holdings held on the record's first day count in the days before it (one bought later had no part in them); an account the record holds later counts only if the record's part works it back on its own. The left-out sentence is DEC-6076's, said of the days before the record only, and only when those days are worked back: "Before Oct 1, 2025, when the daily record begins: Return is on the $X with a price history. <name> ($Y) has no price history, so its gains are not included." Its amounts are today's values, as DEC-6076 has them: $X = today's value of the holdings the days before count; $Y = today's value of each one left out. Example, the account-page drawing's state A: the record begins Oct 1, 2025; 1Y's beginning is Sep 29, 2025; VOO's price history holds $522.43 on Sep 29 and no close again until Dec 31, so VOO moved 0.00% over those days; the bonds were bought Apr 2, 2026, so they had no part. 1Y = (1 + 0.00%) × (1 + 8.26%) − 1 = +8.26%, the same as Since (was +7.12%); 2Y = (522.43 ÷ 460.00) × 1.0826 − 1 = +22.95%, a year over 731 days +10.87% (was +9.57%). Unchanged: a record that begins today (DEC-5291's answer — state D's 1Y +10.00%), a record that reaches back the whole window (the measured return), and a window whose days before the record cannot be worked back (nothing with a history there: DEC-5291's answer, or its refusal).
rows.means: His question, 2026-10-19, on the account-page drawing's state A, and his word "approved." on the fix: join the two methods instead of choosing one. The cause: 1Y opens one day before the daily record begins, so DEC-5291 switched the whole window to the worked-back-from-prices method (holdings with price history only, weighted by today's values), while Since is the measured time-weighted return of the whole account (DEC-4439). It amends DEC-5291 for a record that exists and begins inside the window; the rest of DEC-5291 stands. The Performance tab's v17 phone 1 moves the same way: 1Y +6.10% → +7.46% (= Since), 2Y +11.10% → +11.81% a year. The note under the summary on the account page and the Performance tab, for such a window: "Your daily record begins Oct 1, 2025, so the days before it are worked back from each holding's price history." (it read "Your daily record does not reach back to … yet, so the beginning is worked back from today's values and each holding's price history.", no longer true there).

rows.subject: The class the broker sends decides a holding's class, before its name (Q10, settling DEC-2159 against brief B7)
rows.plain: “always the class broker sends.” For a linked or imported holding, the class the broker sends decides what it is. The name, a maturity date and the app's other automatic rules are used only when the broker sends no usable class. A class the person sets themselves still outranks every automatic rule. Example: a money-market fund the broker flags as cash is Cash; a T-bill ETF the broker sends as an ETF is Stocks / Funds.
rows.means: His answer, 2026-10-20, to the question put to him that two of his rulings conflict on which comes first when deciding an asset's class: its name, or the class the broker sends. The two were brief B7 (DEC-0309, 2026-08-20: the name first, the broker's tag only a fallback) and his Q10 answer (DEC-2159, 2026-09-30: the institution's own class field first), which had not been built because it contradicted B7. Before: the person's own class, then the name, then a maturity date, then the broker's cash-equivalent flag, then the broker's type tag. Now: the person's own class, then the class the broker sends (its cash-equivalent flag, else its type), then the name, a maturity date and the other automatic rules. What moves, as shown to him in the worked example: a money-market fund the broker flags is Cash (it was Stocks / Funds by DEC-0051 and DEC-0092); a bond ETF or T-bill ETF the broker sends as an ETF is Stocks / Funds (it was Bonds & CDs by its name and DEC-0051's T-bill rule); an individual bond or CD the broker sends as a bond stays Bonds & CDs.

A value typed today from a statement dated Sep 30 is booked on Sep 30, not today. Example: a Treasury on record at $24,650, retyped on Oct 20 at $24,900 as of Sep 30. rows.means: The Bonds and Other investments editors let a person date a typed value (Value as of). The daily record was written from today's accounts, so the new value read as a change today. Now the save walks back over the days already recorded, from the latest to the as-of date, and puts the new value on each day that still holds the value being replaced; the daily net worth and cash-plus-investments totals move by the same amount on each day moved. A purchase counts in at what was paid; a sale counts out at what it brought in after its fee. EARLIER WORDING, round 3 of the same day: a sale counted out at the previous evening's value, which gave +8.00% for the first example; replaced within the hour by this rule, so a person can see how the number was made.
